title: Treating Minor Cuts and Burns
hook: Most household cuts and burns heal fine with the right first move — and knowing the few that need a doctor keeps a small injury from becoming a big one.
key_points: For minor cuts: stop the bleeding with gentle pressure, clean with water, then cover.
For minor burns: cool under cool (not ice-cold) running water for about 10–20 minutes.
Don't use ice, butter, or ointments on a fresh burn — they can make it worse.
Seek care for deep, large, or dirty wounds, signs of infection, or burns on the face, hands, or joints.
content_html: Cuts and burns are the small change of household injuries — most are minor and heal on their own. But the first few minutes matter, and a handful of injuries genuinely need a professional.
extra_html: For a minor cut, Mayo Clinic's first-aid guidance is to stop the bleeding with gentle, direct pressure, rinse the wound with clean water, apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly if you like, and cover it to keep it clean. For a minor burn, the key move is to cool it promptly under cool — not ice-cold — running water for about 10 to 20 minutes, then cover it loosely with a clean, non-stick dressing. Avoid the old myths: ice can injure the tissue further, and butter or thick ointments trap heat and invite infection. The other half of first aid is knowing your limits. Seek medical care for wounds that are deep, gaping, or dirty, that won't stop bleeding, or that show signs of infection (spreading redness, warmth, pus, fever) — and for burns that are large, blistering badly, or located on the face, hands, feet, or over a joint.

related.title: Hands-Only CPR
related.hook: If an adult collapses and isn't breathing, you don't need training certificates or rescue breaths — just two steps that can double or triple their chance of survival.

related.title: When a Symptom Needs a Doctor
related.hook: Most everyday symptoms pass on their own. The skill worth having is recognizing the red flags that mean don't wait — call for help now.

flashcards.prompt: What's the right first step for a minor burn?

choices.text: Cool it under cool running water for 10–20 minutes

flashcards.explanation_html: Mayo Clinic advises cooling a minor burn under cool running water; ice can damage tissue, and butter or ointments trap heat and raise infection risk.

flashcards.prompt: When should a cut or burn be seen by a professional?
flashcards.back_html: If it's deep, large, or dirty, won't stop bleeding, shows signs of infection, or a burn covers the face, hands, feet, or joints — get medical care.
